question: What is the main job of an analgesic drug?

options.A: To relieve pain without causing unconsciousness
options.B: To reduce high body temperature quickly
options.C: To put the patient into a deep sleep
options.D: To lower elevated blood pressure readings

explanation: Analgesics are medicines that chase away pain while keeping your patient awake and alert so you can still talk to them! [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h1)

question: Why do nurses say that pain is a subjective experience?

options.A: It disappears completely as soon as vital signs return to normal.
options.B: It can only be accurately measured with laboratory blood tests.
options.C: It always produces visible swelling and redness at the injury site.
options.D: It is felt and described differently by every individual person.

explanation: Pain is personal! What makes one patient cry out might just be a mild discomfort to another. Always trust how your patient says they feel. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h1)

question: Which organ is in the greatest danger during a paracetamol overdose?
explanation: The liver works hard to break down paracetamol. When too much is taken at once, it gets overwhelmed and can suffer serious damage. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h2)

question: A patient with a history of stomach ulcers has joint pain. Which drug group should make you extra careful as a nurse?
explanation: NSAIDs (like ibuprofen) block protective factors in the stomach lining. For a patient with ulcers, this can easily trigger bleeding! [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h2)

question: What happens when you give an opioid antagonist like naloxone?

options.A: It slows down digestion to increase drug absorption.
options.B: It blocks and reverses opioid receptor activity completely.
options.C: It lowers body temperature during a severe fever.
options.D: It stimulates mu receptors to provide deep pain relief.

explanation: Think of naloxone as the ultimate rescue drug. It kicks opioids right off their receptors to instantly reverse dangerous breathing slowdowns. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h3)

question: Why are pure opioid agonists like morphine considered strong pain relievers?

options.A: They fully activate mu receptors to stop severe pain signals.
options.B: They never cause any unwanted side effects in the body.
options.C: They eliminate all inflammation directly at the injury site.
options.D: They only work on mild headaches and minor muscle sprains.

explanation: Morphine locks strongly onto mu receptors in the central nervous system, which is why it's so powerful at knocking out severe pain. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h3)

question: What kind of pain do adjuvant medications like gabapentin usually target?

options.A: Sudden high fever from bacterial infection
options.D: Severe stomach cramping from food poisoning

explanation: Gabapentin and similar drugs are originally seizure medicines, but they work wonders for that burning, shooting pain caused by damaged nerves. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h4)

question: Why do doctors often add co-analgesics to a patient's treatment plan?

options.A: To cause immediate unconsciousness during surgical procedures
options.B: To speed up the physical healing of broken bones and fractures
options.C: To replace all nursing physical assessments of comfort levels
options.D: To target specific pain types and reduce opioid requirements

explanation: By teaming up different types of pain meds, we can tackle stubborn pain better and use lower, safer doses of heavy opioids. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h4)

question: Which medication group forms the first step of the WHO analgesic ladder?
explanation: For mild pain, we always start simple at Step One with basic non-opioids like paracetamol or ibuprofen, plus an adjuvant if needed. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h5)

question: A cancer patient on a Step Two weak opioid still has severe pain. What should you do next?

options.A: Continue the current dose because ladder steps cannot be skipped
options.B: Discontinue all pain medications until the pain resolves naturally
options.C: Encourage the patient to rely strictly on relaxation breathing
options.D: Advocate for moving up to Step Three with a strong opioid

explanation: The pain ladder is flexible! If a weaker step isn't cutting it, it's time to step up to stronger medications to keep the patient comfortable. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h5)

question: Which side effect of opioids do patients almost NEVER build a tolerance to?
explanation: Patients get used to the sleepiness and dizziness over time, but opioids keep slowing down the bowels. Always plan ahead with laxatives! [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h6)

question: Why is an oral dose of an opioid usually higher than its intravenous (IV) dose?

options.A: Intravenous injections bypass the bloodstream completely.
options.B: Intravenous drugs are absorbed much slower by body tissues.
options.C: The digestive tract destroys all active ingredients instantly.
options.D: Oral drugs undergo significant first-pass breakdown in the liver.

explanation: When you swallow a pill, it passes through the liver first and some of the drug gets metabolized. IV drugs skip this trip, so you need less of them! [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h6)

question: What vital sign must you watch most carefully after giving an IV opioid?
explanation: Safety first! Opioids can slow down the brain's breathing center, making your respiratory check the most important assessment in the room. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h7)

question: You gave a patient an oral pain pill at 10:00 AM. When is the best time to check if it worked?
explanation: Oral meds generally take about an hour to hit their peak effect in the body. That's your cue to pop back in and reassess your patient's pain! [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h7)
